title: Memory Safety Instrumentations in Practice: Usability, Performance, and Security Guarantees
problem: Memory safety violations (spatial safety) remain widespread despite extensive research; existing sanitizers promise ease-of-use and low overhead but face adoption challenges due to spurious error reports and practical usability issues.
motivation: C's undefined behavior and spatial safety violations continue causing security breaches; understanding real-world adoption barriers is needed to improve sanitizer design.
method: The paper builds an LLVM-based framework (a compiler tool that instruments code) to systematically test two memory-safety approaches: Low-Fat Pointers and SoftBound. The framework automates the common tasks that these approaches share—figuring out where to add safety checks and removing redundant ones—so researchers can compare them fairly. It then measures what fraction of memory accesses don't actually need checking (are provably safe) and breaks down where the performance cost comes from.
key_novelty: The paper's key idea is an LLVM framework that automates the shared tasks between different memory-safety approaches, making it possible to compare them fairly and identify exactly where practical adoption breaks down.
contributions: Identification of usability pain points in Low-Fat Pointers and SoftBound
Open-source LLVM instrumentation framework for memory safety analysis
Quantitative insights on provably-safe accesses and overhead attribution

metrics.other: spurious error reports, execution overhead, false positive analysis

limitations: Focus on spatial safety only; temporal safety and other C/C++ vulnerabilities not discussed.
primary_theme: practical analysis of memory safety sanitizers
